questions.q: The editorial opens with Helen Keller, blind and deaf from early childhood. According to her words, how is character developed?
options: Through avoiding every difficulty
Not quite. The article says: Not in ease and quiet, but through the experience of trial and suffering.
Through comfort and long rest
Not quite. The article says: Not in ease and quiet, but through the experience of trial and suffering.
Not in ease and quiet, but through the experience of trial and suffering
Yes. Trial strengthens the soul.
Through wealth and good connections
Not quite. The article says: Not in ease and quiet, but through the experience of trial and suffering.
questions.rationale: “Character cannot be developed in ease and quiet. Only through experience of trial and suffering can the soul be strengthened, ambition inspired, and success achieved.”

questions.q: A cow takes in grass and gives out milk. What does the Maulana compare to this?
options: The farmer’s work of turning seed into crops
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s inner system, which turns trouble into patience and relief into gratitude.
The scholar’s habit of turning books into speeches
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s inner system, which turns trouble into patience and relief into gratitude.
The trader’s skill of turning goods into profit
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s inner system, which turns trouble into patience and relief into gratitude.
The believer’s inner system, which turns trouble into patience and relief into gratitude
Right. So both conditions become a blessing.
questions.rationale: “A believer has a special psychological system. This system turns trouble into patience for God and relief into gratitude for God.”

questions.q: “Starve the problems, feed the opportunities.” What does the wise man do, according to the diary?
options: He ignores opportunities until problems disappear
Not quite. The article says: He sets problems aside for the future and puts all his energy into present opportunities.
He divides his energy equally between the two
Not quite. The article says: He sets problems aside for the future and puts all his energy into present opportunities.
He sets problems aside for the future and puts all his energy into present opportunities
Well read. By using opportunities he eventually resolves both.
He solves every problem before doing anything else
Not quite. The article says: He sets problems aside for the future and puts all his energy into present opportunities.
questions.rationale: “The wise man is the one who puts problems into the future and puts all his energy into using the present opportunities.”

questions.q: Dale Carnegie is quoted on what truly takes intelligence in life. What is it?
options: To avoid all risks
Not quite. The article says: To profit from your losses.
To hide your failures
Not quite. The article says: To profit from your losses.
To capitalize on your gains
Not quite. The article says: To profit from your losses.
To profit from your losses
Yes. “Any fool” can capitalize on gains.
questions.rationale: “The most important thing in life is not to capitalize on your gains. Any fool can do that. The really important thing is to profit from your losses.”

questions.q: Which principle does the article call “a master key to human ethics”?
options: Speak little and listen much
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you would like them to treat you.
Treat others as they have treated you
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you would like them to treat you.
Keep to your own people
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you would like them to treat you.
Treat others as you would like them to treat you
Correct. One key for every locked door.
questions.rationale: “Whatever behaviour they want from others, they should themselves accord to others… It is like a master key to human ethics, one single key which suffices to open all locked doors.”

questions.q: Gandhi’s shyness once left him unable to speak in court. What lasting benefit did he say it brought him?
options: It made him a faster writer
Not quite. The article says: It taught him economy of words, so that a thoughtless word hardly ever escaped him.
It taught him economy of words, so that a thoughtless word hardly ever escaped him
Right. A weakness became a strength.
It won him the sympathy of judges
Not quite. The article says: It taught him economy of words, so that a thoughtless word hardly ever escaped him.
It kept him away from public life
Not quite. The article says: It taught him economy of words, so that a thoughtless word hardly ever escaped him.
questions.rationale: “Its greatest benefit has been that it has taught me the economy of words… a thoughtless word hardly ever escaped my tongue or pen.”

questions.article: An Interview with Ms Gul Zeba
questions.q: Ms Gul Zeba grew up in a religious home and had memorized the Quran, yet she felt something was missing. What was it?
options: She was doing all that was expected, but did not feel she truly knew God
Well read. She prayed to be shown a way to know Him better.
She had not yet travelled for study
Not quite. The article says: She was doing all that was expected, but did not feel she truly knew God.
She had no one to teach
Not quite. The article says: She was doing all that was expected, but did not feel she truly knew God.
She had too little time for prayer
Not quite. The article says: She was doing all that was expected, but did not feel she truly knew God.
questions.rationale: “There was a moment in my life when I felt that I was doing all the things a Muslim should do but did not truly know who God was.”

questions.q: The able and upright minister Mahmud Gawan was put to death after envious nobles forged a letter in his name. Which saying of the Prophet does the article quote on jealousy?
options: “Jealousy harms only the one envied”
Not quite. The article says: “Beware of jealousy. Verily, it destroys good deeds the way fire destroys wood”.
“Beware of jealousy. Verily, it destroys good deeds the way fire destroys wood”
Yes. Envy ruined the minister, the king and the kingdom alike.
“Jealousy is the beginning of ambition”
Not quite. The article says: “Beware of jealousy. Verily, it destroys good deeds the way fire destroys wood”.
“Jealousy passes with time”
Not quite. The article says: “Beware of jealousy. Verily, it destroys good deeds the way fire destroys wood”.
questions.rationale: “Beware of jealousy. Verily, it destroys good deeds the way fire destroys wood.”

questions.q: “A good opportunity is seldom presented and is easily lost.” How does the article apply this to the Hereafter?
options: Opportunities continue after death
Not quite. The article says: The chances to prepare for it are given only in this life, and death ends them for all time.
Opportunities come only in old age
Not quite. The article says: The chances to prepare for it are given only in this life, and death ends them for all time.
Only a few people are ever given a chance
Not quite. The article says: The chances to prepare for it are given only in this life, and death ends them for all time.
The chances to prepare for it are given only in this life, and death ends them for all time
Well reasoned. Hence the call to examine our lives now.
questions.rationale: “And then death—the great cut-off point—comes and puts an end to opportunities for all time.”

questions.q: The chapter speaks of those “who are uncharitable even over very small things.” How does the commentary describe such a person?
options: He will not give even what costs him nothing substantial – a matchstick or his good wishes
Exactly. Belief in the reckoning is what makes one considerate.
He gives only when asked twice
Not quite. The article says: He will not give even what costs him nothing substantial – a matchstick or his good wishes.
He gives only to his relatives
Not quite. The article says: He will not give even what costs him nothing substantial – a matchstick or his good wishes.
He gives large sums but in secret
Not quite. The article says: He will not give even what costs him nothing substantial – a matchstick or his good wishes.
questions.rationale: “He will not even give to others such things as will cause him no substantial loss—even if it be only matchsticks or his good wishes.”
